title: Santiago Zapata - Roguelikes as automated Dungeon Masters: a historical overview
speaker: Santiago Zapata
summary: Santiago Zapata traces roguelikes back to Dungeons & Dragons, arguing that the four core traditional-roguelike features (permanent consequences, character-centric play, turn-based play, procedural content) all have tabletop roots. He frames Rogue as a simple automated Dungeon Master and the genre's evolution as an effort to build an ever better private Dungeon Master. He explains how Rogue disguised its limited content (identification, harsh difficulty, food clock, reliance on imagination), defends character-based display as a major legacy, and surveys the eras: 1980s ports and expansions (Hack, Moria, Larn, Omega), 1990s ADOM and the over-ambitious simulation projects, and the 2000s shift to forums, RogueBasin, coffee-break roguelikes and 7DRL.

insights.claim: The four core features of a traditional roguelike (permanent consequences, character-centric play, turn-based play, procedural content) all trace back to Dungeons & Dragons, the shared interest of the early roguelike developers.
insights.detail: Zapata notes Rogue openly uses D&D stats like strength and dexterity, then asks whether D&D itself is a roguelike by checking it against the four features discussed the year before. A tabletop session cannot roll back what happened; D&D turned wargame squads into one character per player; turns came from wargames and the practical need to order players around a game master.
insights.quote: we know that the developers of the early rock legs into the rock had a common interest and it was Dungeons and Dragons

insights.claim: Tabletop Dungeon Master design kits that included tools for generating random adventures were a predecessor of roguelike procedural generators, and covered more than terrain: setting, NPCs and everything in the adventure.
insights.detail: Zapata points out that a Dungeon Master already improvises story as the session unfolds, but the Dungeon Master's design kit went further with sections for creating random adventures. He contrasts this with Rogue, which only creates nine rooms, interconnects them and varies their sizes.
insights.quote: it also included some modules or some sections where they had a lot of tools to create random adventures

insights.claim: Rogue can be understood as a simple, boring automated Dungeon Master, and the evolution of roguelikes as an ongoing attempt to build a better private Dungeon Master.
insights.detail: The automated DM is less capable than a real one but does all the computation, is always available, and needs no friends to run a session, while still letting you brag about your accomplishments. Zapata argues the genre's whole journey, at least for single-player games, has been improving this private DM.
insights.quote: the whole journey of the bell of evolution of roguelike games has been trying to make a better private Dungeon Master every time

insights.claim: Rogue's identification of potions, wands and scrolls made a small fixed content set feel larger, as if the Dungeon Master were inventing new magic items each game.
insights.detail: Zapata lists identification as the first way Rogue's developers overcame their limitations, because the game was in the end pretty simple. Unidentified items gave the impression of more complexity and content than a fixed set.
insights.quote: the discovery mechanics that is been having to identify the potions the wand the scrolls as that gave the impression of having more complexity or more content

insights.claim: Rogue's unusually harsh difficulty, which became a staple of the genre, served to make the simple journey its automated Dungeon Master creates more interesting.
insights.detail: Zapata notes this difficulty spike is not really found in tabletop sessions. Original Rogue is extremely hard to beat; he cites a Roguelike Temple forum thread of a player who has tried to beat it for four or five years without success.
insights.quote: this difficulty spike again is a way to make the journey that the dungeon master is creating more interesting

insights.claim: Rogue's food timer exists to keep pressure on the player to move forward through the dungeon.
insights.detail: Zapata lists the food timer among the devices Rogue used to overcome its limitations, alongside identification and harsh difficulty.
insights.quote: the food timer as an additional mission to keep these the pressure on the player to go ahead and continue on the journey

insights.claim: Rogue's terminal display relied on the player's imagination the way tabletop sessions did, which Zapata calls a happy accident since the developers would have used graphics if they could.
insights.detail: In tabletop games monster manuals had illustrations, but in play everything happened in the players' heads. Terminal displays were what Rogue's developers had, and they became a vehicle for imagination-reliant representation.
insights.quote: which was a happy accident if you ask the developers of Road they say that if they could have made graphics they would have done graphics

insights.claim: Character-based display makes content cheap to create: a new monster needs only a glyph, a colour, a description and data, with no sprite, model or animations for its interactions, which allows complex content and interactions.
insights.detail: Zapata calls character-based display perhaps Rogue's second most important legacy after procedural generation, often missing from definitions because it seems superficial. Because interactions only need describing, not animating, entity interactions can be very complex; doing the same with full graphics is very expensive.
insights.quote: you just decide what character to use what to use and then write the description and then go and define the data for that monster

insights.claim: Replacing ASCII characters with static sprites is a half-measure that players find unsatisfying; either commit fully to graphics, with the cost that entails, or stay with characters.
insights.detail: Zapata argues full graphics for complex interactions is very expensive, and if you do not go all the way players feel it is not enough. He also notes characters ease visual representation of procedurally generated monsters and items and give each player a personal mental image, but concedes modern players want graphics and most of the time you will need them.
insights.quote: either you go all the way or you stay on this safe side

insights.claim: Because Rogue was closed source, the first roguelikes in the 1980s were ports and reverse-engineered recreations, sometimes made from memory after a brief glimpse of Rogue on a university trip, and they gradually added features beyond Rogue.
insights.detail: Communication was limited and games could not be shared over the internet, so people rebuilt Rogue on other machines. These ports then started doing more than Rogue did. Games ran on university computers that students reached via terminal.
insights.quote: rogue closed-source it was the source was not available and people wanted to play rogue so they had to port it to different kind of machines

insights.claim: Hack expanded Rogue in the direction of world interaction, mimicking a Dungeon Master resolving player actions, while Moria expanded it with more content and a Lord of the Rings setting; NetHack and Angband powered up those same two directions.
insights.detail: Hack aimed to make the world feel more interactive, like telling a DM you drink something or pull a lever and hearing the result. Moria added more monsters, letters that represent whole races, and a setting. NetHack continued world interaction and Angband more content and lore.
insights.quote: Huck first tried to do it with world interaction so trying to make the world feel more more interactive again making it feel like this was a dungeon master

insights.claim: Moria was briefly turned into a real-time game, players did not like it, and it reverted to turn-based, showing how a turn structure born of technical constraints became a core design element.
insights.detail: Zapata says this episode is not widely known. The first roguelikes were turn-based because of technical constraints, yet that ended up part of the design and is probably the most contentious part of it today.
insights.quote: he transformed it into a real-time game briefly so it was not a turn-based game for some small time and people just did not like it

insights.claim: Larn was the first roguelike with a town level and varied room types in its generation, and Omega seeded features of 1990s roguelikes such as a countryside and a pantheon of gods.
insights.detail: Larn moved beyond rooms and corridors to more varied kinds of rooms, improving on Hack's few fixed special rooms. Omega is not widely known but included a countryside and gods that later appeared in games like ADOM.
insights.quote: learn was the first to date town level and it also went into the new generation so instead of just having rooms with corridors

insights.claim: Because computers are not good at storytelling, ADOM built a detailed original setting with foundations for several possible paths and let the player fill the gaps in their head to create a richer world.
insights.detail: Zapata (offering his own view, not the developer's) says NetHack was too crazy and Angband too dull, so ADOM created an original setting. The player may or may not follow its paths, and their imagination completes a more complex setting than earlier games had.
insights.quote: computers are really not very good at storytelling so what Adam did was create a general setting

insights.claim: The 1990s ambition to make roguelikes the ultimate detailed simulation of a fantasy world, inspired by GenRogue, largely failed because the projects were too complex for developers to finish.
insights.detail: These games aimed less at being games than at extreme simulation detail, such as combat with 100 body parts modelled down to fingernails. Zapata says this did not work well because they were too complex to complete.
insights.quote: the problem is that this not did not really work too well because they were too complex for the for the developers to complete them

insights.claim: In the 2000s the roguelike community shifted from huge simulations to smaller, focused games, driven by coffee-break roguelikes and the Seven Day Roguelike challenge.
insights.detail: Zapata says this changed the community's mindset toward something smaller and more focused, though projects aiming at great worlds like Ultima Ratio Regum continue. 7DRL went from under 20 roguelikes in the 1980s to hundreds each year, bringing ideas from other genres in.
insights.quote: we had the coffee-break roguelikes happen and the second a roguelike which changed a bit the mindset of the community to try to make something smaller

insights.claim: The flood of 7DRL games exposed roguelikes to wider game-development circles, and the influence then reversed as roguelike elements permeated other genres and mainstream games.
insights.detail: First ideas from other genres were brought into roguelikes through 7DRL; eventually the reverse effect happened.
insights.quote: eventually the reverse effect happened so elements from the roguelikes infected a different different genres permeated different journals and the mainstream games

insights.claim: As Usenet died, roguelike knowledge moved to game-specific forums, RogueBasin (which became the biggest roguelike catalogue and algorithm resource), the roguelike database and Roguelike Temple forums.
insights.detail: Zapata says he had the idea for RogueBasin but most content came from many contributors. In the 1990s the body of knowledge on algorithms and data structures was scattered across websites and Usenet groups.
insights.quote: that was where rogue racing was created and actually I had the idea to create it but most of the content of course come from a lot of contributors
